analysis.one_liner: Gives federal grants to states and cities that guarantee free lawyers to low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2024 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund, authorizing $100 million a year for five years. States, cities, and tribal governments could apply for grants only after passing a law guaranteeing free, full legal representation to tenants earning up to 200% of the poverty line in eviction cases and housing-subsidy termination cases. Federal reviewers would give priority to applicants whose states also limit eviction reasons, require 30-day written notice, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants facing eviction or the loss of a housing subsidy. Today most tenants in eviction court have no lawyer while landlords generally do; a guaranteed attorney means someone to raise defenses, negotiate more time, or challenge improper filings, which can mean the difference between keeping a home and an eviction record that follows a family for years.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund authorized at $100 million per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2029 [S2].

Grants go only to states, local governments, or tribal governments that have enacted legislation providing full legal representation at no cost to tenants earning at or below 200% of the federal poverty line in eviction and subsidy-termination proceedings [S2].

The HUD Secretary must prioritize applicants whose states limit the grounds for eviction, require at least 30 days' written notice, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance, and applicants who use grant funds to recruit and train tenant attorneys [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through up to $500 million in appropriations over five years. Landlords would bear indirect costs: represented tenants contest cases more effectively, and states seeking grant priority would be pushed toward limits on eviction grounds and longer notice periods.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $100 million a year in new federal spending for five years [S2], and grants flow only to governments that first pass their own right-to-counsel laws, so coverage would be uneven and depend on state legislative action rather than being a national guarantee [S2].

The priority rules effectively push states toward specific landlord-tenant policies — limited eviction grounds, 30-day notice, diversion programs — as the price of competing for funds [S2], which critics of such policies view as federal interference with state property law; funds are also authorized, not guaranteed, so annual appropriations battles could leave the fund underfunded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A guaranteed lawyer in eviction court addresses a stark imbalance: landlords almost always have counsel or repeat familiarity with the process, while most tenants do not, and studies cited in state-level debates have shown representation sharply reduces forced moves. The cost is modest by federal standards ($500 million over five years) but real, and the design outsources the core guarantee to states, so tenants' rights would depend on where they live. The federal leverage over state eviction laws is the most contestable part.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2024 and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on July 9, 2024, joined by Sens. Van Hollen, Wyden, Warren, and Sanders [S1][S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — is recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords are better off: tenants will continue to face eviction proceedings largely without lawyers, preserving the practical advantage landlords hold in most cases. The Treasury also saves the $500 million that would have been appropriated.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Van Hollen, Wyden, Warren, and Sanders
for.role: Original cosponsors (4 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents)

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 9, 2024 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats or independents; no senator is recorded as opposing it, because no one ever had to vote — the bill died from committee inaction, not from a recorded fight.

industries.note: Guaranteed counsel would let tenants raise defenses, demand proof, and negotiate more time, weakening the practical edge landlords now hold in eviction court. The bill also rewards states that restrict eviction grounds and extend notice periods, further limiting landlord flexibility.
Grants would fund recruitment, training, and the cost of representing covered tenants, expanding paid legal work dedicated to low-income tenants' interests.
